subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Recording crime through official police statistics has which key weakness?
options: Many crimes go unreported, creating a 'dark figure' of crime
questions.explain: Official statistics miss unreported and undetected offences, known as the dark figure of crime.

questions.q: Bandura's Bobo doll study is often used to support which explanation of aggression and crime?
questions.explain: Bandura's Bobo doll study showed children imitate aggression they observe, supporting social learning theory.

questions.q: Punishment is intended to reduce criminal behaviour mainly by doing what?
questions.explain: Punishment aims to deter offending by making the consequences of crime unpleasant.

questions.q: According to Eysenck, the criminal personality scores highly on which dimensions?
questions.explain: Eysenck proposed that high extraversion, neuroticism and psychoticism characterise the criminal personality.

questions.q: A behaviour can be deviant but not criminal. Which is the best example?
options: Talking loudly to yourself in public
questions.explain: Talking loudly to yourself breaks social norms (deviant) but is not against the law (not criminal).

questions.q: A biological explanation of criminality suggests crime may be linked to what?
questions.explain: Biological explanations link criminality to inherited genes and differences in brain structure or function.

questions.q: A weakness of purely biological explanations of crime is that they may ignore what?
options: The role of upbringing and environment
questions.explain: Biological accounts can be reductionist, neglecting social and environmental influences on offending.

questions.q: Anger-management programmes try to reduce reoffending by doing what?
options: Teaching offenders to control emotional responses
questions.explain: Anger management teaches offenders to recognise and control emotional triggers, reducing reoffending.

questions.q: The idea that a harsh upbringing or poor role models contributes to crime is part of which explanation?
questions.explain: Social explanations emphasise upbringing, environment and role models in the development of criminal behaviour.

questions.q: Social learning theory explains criminal behaviour as being learned through what?
questions.explain: Social learning theory says criminal behaviour can be learned by observing and imitating role models.

questions.q: Token economy programmes used with offenders are based on which principle?
questions.explain: Token economies reward desired behaviour with tokens that can be exchanged for privileges, reinforcing good conduct.

questions.q: The XYY 'supermale' theory suggested some criminality might be linked to what?
questions.explain: The XYY theory proposed that an extra Y chromosome was associated with increased aggression and offending.

questions.q: Which of these aims mainly to change behaviour and reintegrate an offender rather than just punish?
questions.explain: Rehabilitation aims to reform offenders and help them reintegrate, reducing future offending.

questions.q: What is the difference between crime and deviance?
options: Crime breaks the law; deviance breaks social norms
questions.explain: Crime is behaviour that breaks the law, while deviance is behaviour that goes against social norms.

questions.q: Lombroso's theory of the 'born criminal' claimed offenders could be identified by what?
questions.explain: Lombroso argued criminals were a throwback (atavistic) type identifiable by physical features such as a strong jaw.

questions.q: A criticism of using punishment alone to reduce crime is that it may do what?
options: Fail to teach better behaviour and cause resentment
questions.explain: Punishment alone may not teach alternative behaviour and can lead to resentment or further offending.

questions.q: Differences in brain structure and function feature in which type of explanation of crime?
questions.explain: Differences in brain structure and function are part of biological explanations of criminal behaviour.

questions.q: A major criticism of Lombroso's theory is that it was what?
options: Based on flawed methods and lacked a proper control group
questions.explain: Lombroso's work has been heavily criticised for poor scientific method and failing to use a non-criminal control group.

questions.q: In social learning theory, being rewarded for behaviour seen in others is called what?
questions.explain: Vicarious reinforcement is learning to repeat behaviour because we see it rewarded in others.

questions.q: Why is defining crime difficult across cultures and time?
options: What counts as a crime varies between societies and changes over time
questions.explain: Definitions of crime differ between cultures and shift over time, so crime is socially and historically relative.

questions.q: A strength of biological explanations of crime is that they are often supported by what?
options: Scientific evidence such as twin and brain studies
questions.explain: Biological explanations gain support from scientific research like twin studies and brain-imaging evidence.

questions.q: Eysenck argued that high-extraversion individuals seek more stimulation because their nervous system is what?
questions.explain: Eysenck suggested extraverts are chronically under-aroused, so they seek stimulation, which may lead to risk-taking.
